bib.title: PromptBench: A Unified Library for Evaluation of Large Language Models

read.skipped: reference list skimmed only for lineage

question: How can LLM evaluation (standard, adversarial-prompt, prompt-engineering and dynamic) be done in one unified, extensible research library?
contributions: A unified Python library for LLM evaluation with modules for models, datasets, prompts, prompt engineering, adversarial prompt attacks, evaluation protocols and analysis tools
Support for standard, dynamic (DyVal) and semantic (MSTemp) evaluation protocols
Leaderboards for adversarial prompt attack, prompt engineering and dynamic evaluation

method.summary: PromptBench is a modular Python library (pip install promptbench) wrapping model loading (LLMModel/VLMModel), dataset loading (DatasetLoader), prompts, six prompt-engineering methods, four levels of adversarial prompt attack, and standard/dynamic/semantic protocols. A four-step pipeline loads a dataset, specifies a model, defines prompts, and defines input/output processing plus a metric. Benchmark results (Figs 3-5) are shown only as partial plots.
method.task: LLM evaluation tooling: robustness to adversarial prompts, prompt engineering comparison, dynamic evaluation

datasets.name: GLUE (SST-2, CoLA, QQP, MRPC, MNLI, QNLI, RTE, WNLI)
DyVal (dynamic protocol, generated on the fly)
datasets.size: 7 reasoning tasks (arithmetic, linear equation, boolean, deductive, abductive logic, reachability, max sum path)

inference.max_tokens: max_new_tokens is a parameter of LLMModel; example uses max_new_tokens=10 (Fig 2)
inference.samples: Few-shot: three randomly chosen training examples per task. Runs and seeds for Figs 3-5 not stated.
inference.prompting: Four prompt types: task-oriented and role-oriented, each zero-shot or few-shot. Six prompt-engineering methods: CoT, zero-shot CoT, EmotionPrompt, Expert Prompting, Generated Knowledge, Least to Most.

parameters.attacks: character: TextBugger, DeepWordBug; word: BertAttack, TextFooler; sentence: StressTest, CheckList; semantic: simulated regional linguistic styles. Attack budgets and thresholds not given.

other.fig3_metric: Average PDR (+5) per dataset, axis 0-80, read from Fig 3; PDR is not defined in the text

metrics.name: accuracy (pb.Eval.compute_cls_accuracy)
metrics.definition: classification accuracy of predictions against labels

metrics.name: Average PDR
metrics.definition: not defined in the text; plotted in Fig 3 as Average PDR (+5)

baselines: Baseline prompt vs CoT, Zero-Shot CoT, EmotionPrompt, Expert Prompting (Fig 4)
eval.protocol: Standard (direct inference), dynamic (DyVal) and semantic (MSTemp). Benchmark results are partial and given only as figures; no tables, seeds or significance tests.

prompts.text: Determine if the given pair of statements can be considered the same by responding with 'equivalent' or 'not equivalent'.

As an instrument for question comparison evaluation, consider the questions and determine if their meaning is the same, responding with 'equivalent' for similar questions or 'not equivalent' for different questions.
Review the sentence below and identify whether its grammar is 'Acceptable' or 'Unacceptable': Here are three examples. [three Sentence/Answer pairs]

Functioning as a grammar evaluation tool, analyze the given sentence and decide if it is grammatically correct, responding with 'acceptable' or 'unacceptable': Here are three examples. [three Sentence/Answer pairs]
Classify the sentence as positive or negative: {content}

limits: The paper concedes it may not cover all evaluation scenarios and some metrics might miss nuanced performance differences.
Benchmark results (Figs 3-5) are partial, figure-only, with no numbers, seeds, temperature, attack budgets or definition of PDR.
The library description omits which model versions, decoding settings and prompt sets underlie the leaderboards.
Model list and dataset counts reflect late 2023 to 2024.
